DaVinci Resolve + Local AI Workstation

A complete, scripted post-production workstation: OpenCode driven by a fully local LLM, operating DaVinci Resolve Studio through three MCP servers, with Blender rendered headless for titles and generated content, and a live observability dashboard — on one Apple Silicon Mac, no cloud, no API keys for the editor path.

People kept asking how the setup works; this repo is the answer, as scripts.

│  OpenCode     (opencode — the agent IS the model you run locally)                         │

What each piece brings

Tool Benefit
Splash 1.7.0 (incoai/tap, brew) Local LLM engine serving Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S (262k context, GGUF/IQ3 quant) behind OpenAI and Anthropic-compatible APIs. Persistent disk prefix-cache reuses a fresh session's shared prefix at ~99.7% (measured 2026-11-17: 9,664 of 9,690 tokens served to a different session, 125 ms; production agent prefixes run ~20–45k by that same path). On 1.7.0: TTFT 110–118 ms warm / 291 ms cold, ladder single-stream 219.8 tok/s (probe decode ~170), aggregate plateau 479–494 tok/s across widths 8→32 with the peak at width 4 (526.5). Also hosts a built-in chat UI on :8000.
OpenCode (opencode.ai) The agentic operator. Reads the timeline, plans edits, executes them through MCP with dry-run/confirm-token discipline, verifies via read-backs, renders, grades its own output with ffprobe. Nothing leaves the machine. Replaced Claude Code on 2026-11-16 on measured evidence — see HARNESS-MIGRATION.md.
Community davinci-resolve MCP (samuelgursky/davinci-resolve-mcp) The hands: ~36 action-dispatch tools over the whole scripting API — media pool, timelines, ripple edits with dry-run plans, markers, Fusion comps, render queue + verified outputs (ffprobe cross-check of every render), and a live api_truth knowledge base of verified Resolve API quirks. Destructive ops auto-archive timelines first.
davinci-resolve-advanced MCP (same project) The forensic layer: closed-Project.db reads/writes (captions, speed ramps), .drx grade XML, DRT timelines, FCPXML/EDL/AAF conform, deliverable-QC specs — all without Resolve running.
Official ResolveMCP (bundled in Resolve Studio 21.1+) Blackmagic's own 18-tool surface: canonical and versioned with the app; useful cross-check and fallback.
Brave Search MCP (opt-in: official @brave/brave-search-mcp-server, MIT) The research leg — the only one that costs money: live fact-checks no model can know, like whether a new Resolve build changed an API behaviour or whether an upstream release has wheels on PyPI yet. Priced $5 per 1,000 queries, with $5 of free credit applied automatically every month (~1,000 free queries; card required at signup even for free use). The only leg where queries leave the machine — search strings get the same scrubbing discipline as commit messages. Setup, pricing details and a plan-bound-key gotcha in mcp/mcp-config.md.
splash-dashboard (rickhuizinga/splash-dashboard) Live engine observability on :8280: KV residency, prefix-cache hit rate, admission pacing, decode batch widths — the instrument panel that turns "the model feels slow" into numbers.
Prometheus + Grafana (opt-in; not installed by install.sh) History leg: the engine serves native Prometheus text at /metrics (~130 splash_* series). If you have already installed and provisioned Prometheus + Grafana, the launcher starts them (--no-metrics skips). A fresh machine does not get them automatically — one-time setup is required (start.sh header comments spell out the Grafana 13 provisioning gotcha: [paths] provisioning = … plus permitted_provisioning_paths, or provisioning silently loads nothing). Until then the live dashboard on :8280 is sufficient.
Blender (LTS, at /Applications) Content forge: 3D title stings, extruded logos, generated media — scripted headless (--background --python), rendered transparent-EXR, imported into Resolve as sequence clips with straight alpha. See blender/.
ffmpeg / ffprobe (brew) The verification layer: every render gets probed (frame count, codecs, duration) before it's trusted; sequence encoding; frame extraction for visual checks.
whisper.cpp / whisper CLI (brew + MCP-integrated) Local transcription; the MCP server also feeds transcripts into timeline subtitle tracks and cut-candidate proposals.
Vision add-on (opt-in: install.sh --vision, see vision/) Face-level signals off Resolve: OpenCV YuNet + SFace for detection/identity and MediaPipe for landmarks, in their own Python 3.12 venv. 90 faces detected on one 8.1K frame in 0.29 s (0.96 s with embeddings, 0.0 s model init), 83 of them landed 478 landmarks + 52 ARKit blendshapes in another 0.3 s — so "whose mouth was open during this solo" becomes a JSON query. Opt-in because it's a second venv (~560 MB + ~52 MB models); every weight it installs has a stated licence.
macmon (brew) Zero-overhead Apple GPU/memory/ANE telemetry in a second terminal — watch unified-memory pressure while Resolve renders and the engine serves, which is how the 56 GB memory budget below was chosen.

Which Resolve MCP to use

  • Day-to-day agent work (timeline edits, markers, Fusion, render queue, verified outputs): community davinci-resolve. It has the dry-run / confirm-token / auto-archive guardrails.
  • Closed-project forensics (Project.db, .drx grades, DRT, conform without Resolve open): davinci-resolve-advanced.
  • Canonical Blackmagic surface / cross-check / fallback: official DaVinci Resolve (ships inside Studio 21.1+).

Most sessions use the community server as primary and keep the official one registered as a safety net. Details and registration steps are in mcp/mcp-config.md.

Do not run a blanket pip install -U inside the community server's venv — it carries its own pins (mcp SDK 1.30.0 plus a torch/transformers stack). The only update path is npx -y davinci-resolve-mcp@latest sync; see Verified stack.

Quick start

Requirements

  • Apple Silicon Mac, ideally ≥48 GB unified memory (tuned here on 96 GB; the engine prints its own recommended working set on smaller ones).
  • DaVinci Resolve Studio required for external scripting (the path this launcher and the stdio MCP servers use). The free edition reaches the community server only via the in-app bridge (Workspace ▸ Scripts) on 21.0.x; Resolve 21.1 moved Python scripting to Studio, so from 21.1 on even that bridge path is gone. The official Blackmagic MCP always needs Studio.
  • In Resolve Studio set Preferences → System → General → External scripting using to Local, then restart Resolve if it is already open. Without this the community MCP servers cannot connect.
  • macOS with Homebrew; Python 3.11+; Node 20+. install.sh stops and tells you if Homebrew is missing; it installs Node via Homebrew when absent, but expects a Python 3.11+ already available (the MCP installer requires it).
  • Optional Blender LTS: brew install --cask blender (or download from blender.org). install.sh checks for it and prints this hint, but never installs it itself.
git clone https://github.com/willturner-maker/resolve-ai-workflow.git
cd resolve-ai-workflow
bash install.sh            # everything below, wired into OpenCode
bash install.sh --vision   # same, plus the opt-in face/mouth layer (vision/README.md)
bash install.sh --lsp      # + LSP tool & post-edit diagnostics for OpenCode V2 (project-scoped)

# After install, open a NEW terminal — the launchers arrive on PATH as:
start.sh                   # Splash → dashboard → metrics (opt) → Resolve → OpenCode
stop.sh                    # clean shutdown (leaves Resolve alone)

# From the clone, without relying on PATH:
bash start.sh
bash stop.sh

# Thinking depth for the launch (the default is `medium`; the engine applies it
# to any request that asks for none — the Chat UI and OpenCode both send none):
bash start.sh --xhigh      # deepest deliberation (~3x thinking tokens, ~40% slower)
bash start.sh --low        # or --high; also accepts --effort=<value> / REASONING_EFFORT=<value>

First start: the model download is tens of GB and can take several minutes; subsequent starts take seconds. Watch the terminal until the dashboard URL appears and OpenCode opens.

Disk: the model itself is a one-time download. The persistent prefix cache can grow up to MAX_CACHE_DISK (default 256 G). An external SSD is recommended for the cache — see the EXTERNAL_CACHE variable in start.sh.

First-run checklist

  1. bash install.sh finishes and prints the registered MCP servers (the three Resolve names — plus brave-search if you opted in).
  2. Open a new terminal so PATH picks up the launchers.
  3. start.sh — first start downloads the model; later starts begin in seconds.
  4. The dashboard comes up on :8280, then OpenCode opens. Resolve is not launched: the MCP starts it headless (-nogui) on the first Resolve tool call (open the GUI yourself whenever you want a handoff).
  5. Verify the servers: opencode mcp list — expect the three Resolve names.
  6. Optional: macmon in a second terminal to watch unified-memory pressure.
  7. Confirm the MCP path with a read-only probe — in OpenCode ask: List the timelines in the current Resolve project (read-only). (The probe needs a project open; the agent can create or load one headless.) A reply naming your timelines means the whole chain (engine → MCP → Resolve) works.

If the engine never becomes ready: tail ~/Library/Logs/splash/splash.err.log (the dashboard leg logs to ~/splash-dashboard.log). If MCP servers are missing: re-run npx -y davinci-resolve-mcp@latest setup --clients opencode, then opencode mcp list to confirm and restart the session. If memory pressure turns red: lower MAX_MEMORY and restart (sizing table below).

The dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:8280 shows engine status, KV residency, and cache hit rate — the fastest way to confirm Splash is healthy before talking to the agent.

First start downloads the model (tens of GB) into Splash's cache and can take several minutes. Subsequent starts are seconds once the weights are cached.

The launcher's memory numbers are tunable without editing the script. Defaults are sized for a 96 GB machine running Resolve concurrently; smaller machines should lower them (see table below).

# example for a 64 GB machine
MAX_MEMORY=32G MAX_CACHE_DISK=64G start.sh

# or with the prefix cache on a fast external SSD
MAX_MEMORY=56G MAX_CACHE_DISK=128G EXTERNAL_CACHE="/Volumes/YourSSD/splash-cache" start.sh

Suggested starting points by machine size (the engine also prints its own recommended working set at startup):

Unified memory Suggested MAX_MEMORY Suggested MAX_CACHE_DISK Notes
96 GB 56G (default) 256G (default) Measured on M5 Ultra + Resolve — 256G is the value since 64G saturated and started evicting warm prefixes
64 GB 32–40G 64G Leave headroom for Resolve
48 GB 24–28G 32–64G Watch system pressure; engine recommendation is authoritative

Rough disk use on first run:

  • Model weights (Splash cache): tens of GB (one-time download)
  • Persistent prefix cache: up to the MAX_CACHE_DISK value (default 256G; lives under ~/Library/Caches/Splash/ unless EXTERNAL_CACHE points elsewhere)
  • Vision add-on (opt-in): ~560 MB venv + ~52 MB models
  • Blender: separate application install

Optional hardening: bash tools/precommit-scan.sh --install enables the local-string guard described under Operating practices — worth wiring up before you commit anything of your own into a clone.

  • start.sh / stop.sh — the exact scripts this workstation runs (with the memory-tuning log in the header comments: why 56 GB working set / 128 GB disk cache on a 96 GB machine next to a running Resolve).
  • mcp/mcp-config.md — how the three Resolve MCP servers (plus the optional brave-search research companion) are registered, verified and updated, and why all of them are kept side by side.
  • blender/ — the title pipeline: exr_title_demo.py + a README of every Blender 5.x gotcha and the Resolve import specifics (multi-path EXR import, Alpha mode → Straight, end-exclusive append frames, proof-render verification).
  • vision/ — opt-in face/mouth analysis: install-vision.sh (pinned 3.12 venv + MediaPipe model downloads) and face_probe.py (frame → JSON), plus the measured numbers, the three API rules that cost the most time, and the privacy rules.

What agentic control actually does here

Not a demo reel — production tasks this stack has completed end to end:

  • Editorial surgery with receipts: ripple-inserts and lifts planned by dry-run, executed under confirm tokens, verified by geometry read-back (every item's start/end re-measured), timeline auto-archived before the mutation.
  • Renders that verify themselves: queue job → Complete → verify_output probed the file → caught a "Complete" job that produced a near-empty stub. The agent trusts the probe, never the status line.
  • Fusion comp scripting: keyframe a live comp via script, then prove the change by rendering frames — stills grabs lie about comp output; renders are truth.
  • Bulk triage: color-flag dozens of clips in one call, marker-driven review reports, transcript-driven cut proposals (filler/pause detection) that a human approves before anything is cut.
  • Blender ↔ Resolve round trips: script a 3D logo sting, render 90 UHD transparent frames overnight, import, set straight alpha, ripple-insert at the master head, proof-render 420 frames over the seam, sample frames to confirm.
  • Cross-tool forensics: closed-project DB reads (captions, speed ramps) and conform imports validated without disturbing the live session.

What the vision layer gets you (opt-in)

The Resolve MCP can already transcribe and analyse media, but face-level questions were either Resolve's own black-box AI or nothing at all. This layer makes them scriptable, offline and inspectable — one command, JSON out, no Resolve round trip.

What it does now, measured on a real 8128×4288 anamorphic HEVC frame from a choral recording (M5 Ultra, pinned versions, re-runnable with vision/face_probe.py):

Stage Result Wall
Detection, native-resolution tiles (OpenCV YuNet) 90 faces on one frame 0.29 s (0.96 s including SFace embeddings; 0.0 s model init)
Landmarks + blendshapes on native crops (MediaPipe) 83 of 90 landed 478 landmarks + 52 ARKit blendshapes 0.30 s (~3.4 ms/face)
End to end 90 faces, mouth state on most of them 2.19 s cold, whole process (imports included)

Concrete benefits:

  • Who was actually singing. jawOpen per face per frame cross-checks a solo against the audio — the question a bad boom choice or a spill from the next stand makes expensive to answer by eye. Feed the JSON to the marker/subtitle tools and an agent can propose where to look instead of scrubbing.
  • Coverage signals without a human viewer: faces per frame (wide vs tight, whether a take has anyone's face at all), and with opt-in embeddings, distinct-people counts.
  • A pre-flight content pass: sample N frames per clip before an agent proposes cuts or picks an angle.
  • A blendshape is the right mouth signal, not a lip gap. Measured disagreement on exactly the case that matters: a singer holding a rounded vowel read jawOpen 0.43 while a vertical inner-lip gap read 0.02 — open, puckered (mouthPucker 0.998), and the geometric shortcut calls it shut.

Three rules it encodes, because each one cost debugging time: neither library finds faces on a downscaled wide shot (MediaPipe returned 0 faces at a 1600 px and a 4032 px cap on a frame holding 90+ — its detector is fixed-input, so a face's share of the frame is what matters); so detect on native tiles, then landmark on native crops (same frame: 0 faces whole-frame, 6/6 on crops); and MediaPipe 1.x dropped mp.solutions.* — Tasks API names only, min_face_presence_confidence not min_presence_confidence, and OpenCV arrays must be wrapped in mp.Image. Full set in vision/.

Honest limits: landmark coverage is pose-dependent (83/92 on a frontal riser, 0/3 on a wide shot where people were in profile or facing away — a low count is usually the shot); the mouth threshold comes from one session (n=1, faces ~47–95 px: 0.24–0.73 singing, ≤0.03 at rest); MediaPipe Pose caps at 3 people per call, so never count a crowd with pose.

Privacy: face geometry and 128-d SFace embeddings are identity data. The default output carries boxes, scores and scalar mouth state only; vectors appear solely with --save-embeddings, which prints a warning naming the file. They stay out of repos, pages and deliverables — the publish-scan below blocks names; identity data needs the stricter rule of not being exported at all, especially for footage with minors. Model weights are downloaded from Google's MediaPipe storage and the OpenCV Zoo; nothing here uploads anything.

Transcription: which tool, and where the models live

Three local options, chosen by the question rather than by model size:

Question Use Cost
"What was said, roughly when" — subtitles, search, cut candidates whisper.cpp (installed by install.sh; the MCP server's subtitle and cut-proposal tools ride on those transcripts) base weights ≈ 150 MB, no Python env
Word-level grounding — which word lands at which frame, per-singer timing behind a marker or a zoom cue WhisperX (CTranslate2 large-v3 + wav2vec2 CTC alignment) 4.2 GB weights + ≈1.5 GB venv (torch rides along)

Word-level alignment is the only reason to have WhisperX; faster-whisper's segment timestamps cover everything else. Measured on real multitrack choral audio, M5 Ultra, CPU, int8: 167 s of audio in 48.6 s, a 46-minute act in 638 s (≈4× faster than realtime) — and that is the ASR pass alone; alignment is a second sweep over the same audio.

One shared model cache, not one per project. WhisperX reaches HuggingFace through two channels that expect different paths, and the mismatch is silent — it simply re-downloads ≈4.4 GB:

  • whisperx.load_model(..., download_root=X) uses X directly as its hub dir → X/models--Systran--faster-whisper-large-v3/…
  • the alignment pipeline goes through transformers, which honours HF_HOME → $HF_HOME/hub/models--jonatasgrosman--…/…

So both must point at the same directory, kept on a media volume rather than the boot disk:

export WHISPERX_HF="/Volumes/YourVolume/local.AI/WhisperX/hf"  # ~4.2 GB, reused by every project
export HF_HOME="$WHISPERX_HF"          # before importing whisperx, not after

Put those two exports in the venv's bin/activate as well as the shell profile, so a fresh environment cannot forget them.

Two tidy-ups cut 2.1 GB from the 6.4 GB download: the alignment repo ships five weight formats plus a fairseq n-gram decoding LM, and the HF CTC pipeline loads exactly one of each (keep model.safetensors + config/vocab/preprocessor; drop pytorch_model.bin, lm.binary, unigrams.txt). When pruning, remove a snapshot entry together with the blob it points at, then look for blobs no snapshot references — a half-pruned repo leaves ~800 MB behind that nothing reports as stale.

Benchmarks (measured, reproducible, honest)

The stack ships with its own benchmark practice — full docs, scripts and raw JSONL at https://github.com/willturner-maker/benchmarks. Headlines:

  • Agentic correctness (current series, 2026-11-17h baseline): seven briefs × 3 trials = 21 sessions per pass, graded only from independent read-backs of Resolve state: 21/21 outcomes verified, 21/21 honest reports in the clean pass (MCP 5.3.1 / OpenCode v2.3.0 / Resolve 21.2; a first pass carrying a disclosed context deviation scored 20/21 and is kept as record, not headline). The Claude-era ladder stays quoted separately at 126/126 (MCP 4.18.5–4.19.0, Resolve 21.1.2–21.2) and is never blended with these rows.
  • Follow-up waves, split-reported: a 42-session friction A/B (Tier 3, 2026-11-18k: 42/42 honest, 40/42 verified — the one flip was a recorded repetition collapse, and the tested naming rule was reverted on pre-committed criteria), and a frontier brief (Tier 4, 2026-11-18l, n=6: geometry 6/6, honesty 6/6, outcome split 0 preserved-native / 6 destroyed-then-repaired — verification discipline at ceiling, path discovery at zero).
  • Operation latency (server-side medians): timeline probe ~11 ms, render-job prepare ~130 ms, output verification ~40 ms, timeline-set ~100 ms.
  • Render probe (121-frame UHD H.264 from an 8K source): cold ~3.1 s, warm ~1.2–1.3 s (~93–100 fps), stable run to run single-tenant.
  • Engine (Splash 1.7.0, re-measured 2026-11-17 across three passes, plus a zero-tenancy clean-window pass the same day): TTFT 110–118 ms warm / 291 ms cold; ladder w1 219.8 tok/s (clean window: 225.2, best recorded), plateau 479–494 tok/s across widths 8→32 with the aggregate peak back at width 4 (526.5; clean window 543.8, best recorded); KV admission still paces gracefully — zero suspensions at 611k prompt tokens (3.93× a 155,648-token resident budget, itself +18.8% on 1.6.1) with the quietest demote path on record (+11 blocks total, zero spill).

Version-to-version reruns are scripted (ladder_kv.py runs both concurrency methods in one pass), which is how upgrades get trusted — including the time an upstream bug we filed (#343) came back fixed and got verified by direct probe the same day it shipped.

Operating practices that keep it trustworthy

  1. Dry-run first — the MCP server defaults destructive ops to plans; read the plan.
  2. Read-back beats return values — the Resolve API can say True and do nothing; the server's verification layer and api_truth encode that scar tissue.
  3. Render jobs bind to the CURRENT timeline — pin before mutating; keep render timing measurements single-tenant (concurrency inflates them, e.g. 1.2 s → 7.3 s under a second agent).
  4. Never restart the serving engine mid-suite — the agent is the engine; restarting it ends the session.
  5. Work + scratch off the boot volume — render outputs, preview renders and chooser scratch live on external volumes; the boot disk keeps model weights and the engine KV cache. Configure Resolve's cache locations once (see the MCP's storage guidance), and pass EXTERNAL_CACHE to the launcher for the Splash disk cache on a fast external SSD.
  6. Publish-safe by pre-commit scan — tools/precommit-scan.sh refuses content, file paths and commit messages that would leak home paths, named volumes, camera/reel filenames, credential shapes, emails, or client/project names (deny terms live in .git/info/precommit-terms, never committed). bash tools/precommit-scan.sh --install wires both hooks; --all audits the whole tree. A property description beats a name: "8128×4288 HEVC Main 10, 56 min" tells a reader more than a camera-generated filename ever did — and if you try to quote such a filename here, the guard refuses the commit. A fresh clone does not receive the deny list or the hooks: run bash tools/precommit-scan.sh --install and maintain your own terms in .git/info/precommit-terms if you want the same scrubbing.
  7. Identity data isn't publishable — the scan blocks names; face geometry and face embeddings need the harder rule: never export them at all. Vision probes default to boxes + scores + scalar mouth state, write vectors only when you pass --save-embeddings, and their scratch lives in a per-project directory on a work volume, deleted when the job closes. Footage with minors: treat any derived face data as not-for-export.
  8. Grading is read-backs, not claims — any agent's "done" gets a probe (ffprobe / item geometry / pixel diff of rendered frames) before it counts.

Troubleshooting quick hits

  • No current timeline on a fresh project → create via media_pool.create_timeline.
  • MCP behaves like the old version after an update → the running process predates the sync; /mcp → reconnect both servers; proof is the tool count, not the version string.
  • An empty reply (content: null, or "") from a small max_tokens request is usually the thinking budget crowding out the visible side, not a broken engine: reasoning tokens count inside completion_tokens. Measured 2026-11-22 on the pinned stack: max_tokens=16 → completion_tokens=16 with reasoning_tokens=16 and content=null; the same prompt at max_tokens=200 → READY. with 23 reasoning tokens. So correctness-sensitive requests need room (≥256 in practice) or thinking off for that request — and the opposite applies to bench stages that deliberately send 8-token completions: they measure prompt-side accounting only, never the answer.
  • Engine not answering → tail -f ~/Library/Logs/splash/splash.err.log; first run downloads the model.
  • Port 8000 busy → the launcher kills prior instances by pidfile/name; stop.sh first.
  • Resolve free edition → Workspace ▸ Scripts ▸ resolve_bridge; the community server auto-uses it on 21.0.x.
  • Vision probe returns 0 faces on a big frame → you're asking a detector to see a 1 % face. Run at native resolution (--tile auto), then let stage 2 crop; see the two-stage rule in vision/README.md.
  • Server's strata_run(analyzers=['face']) says it can't run → mediapipe/opencv belong to the server venv there: bash vision/install-vision.sh --mcp-server-venv <server venv>, then /mcp → reconnect.
  • Brave MCP connects but every search returns nothing → the key belongs to the Answers plan, not Search — keys are plan-bound; see mcp/mcp-config.md.
  • Do you still have the Fusion comp you attached? Unknown until you check — survival across a project switch is not deterministic, and the two benchmark waves disagree in a way worth knowing:
    • 2026-11-17g: all six T8 trials read comp-count 1 in-wave and 0 afterwards (project close/load churn during grading, no Resolve restart).
    • 2026-11-17h: all three T8 trials read 1 in-wave and 1 post-wave — same grader, same project-load pattern, comps created both through timeline_item_fusion.add_comp and through the scripting bridge. So: never assume either direction. After any project_manager.load, re-verify with timeline_item_fusion.get_comp_count; if it reads 0, the comp is gone — re-attach (add_comp) and rebuild. (Correction, same day: an earlier version of this note claimed comps "do not survive" project churn. That was the 17g reading stated too strongly; 17h disproved the universal form. The benchmark grades T8 from an in-trial snapshot precisely because the outcome is not predictable, and keeps the post-wave read as product-behavior data.)

Safe update: npx -y davinci-resolve-mcp@latest sync, then /mcp → reconnect both servers. When a major version changed, re-run a benchmark before trusting the numbers. Never pip install -U inside the community server's venv — it carries its own pins.

Splash upgrades need a warm-up pass, not just a restart. A minor Splash bump can reset the engine's persistent prefix cache (1.7.0 did: took back 0 restore points … 0 MiB in the startup log), which silently depresses every performance number until the cache refills. Re-run the suite once unscored, then read /status: when cache.cold_misses stops moving and hit_rate is back above ~0.98, the engine is warm and the next pass is the one you publish.

Verified stack

For the live 2026-11-18 state — including the harness, now OpenCode v2.3.1 — skip to the dated entries below, newest last; Claude Code 2.1.319 in the list below is that earlier snapshot, predating the 2026-11-16 migration (HARNESS-MIGRATION.md), not the current harness:
